title: Apostille FAQ: Common U.S. Questions, Answered
description: Answers to the most common U.S. apostille questions: which office, cost, timing, FBI checks, birth certificates, photocopies, expiry and translations, each cited to an official source.
summary: Most apostille mistakes come from sending a document to the wrong office or skipping a prep step. State-issued or state-notarized documents are apostilled by that state; federal documents such as FBI background checks are apostilled by the U.S. Department of State for $20. Where official sources don't give an answer, this page says so instead of guessing.
items: An apostille is a certificate under the 1961 Hague Apostille Convention that confirms the origin of a public document: the signature, the capacity of the person who signed it and any seal. It does not certify what the document says. It is used when the document will be presented in another country that is party to the Convention.
Where do I get an apostille in the U.S.?

It depends on who signed the document. Documents issued by a state, county or city, or notarized by a state-commissioned notary, go to the apostille office of that state (see the directory). Documents signed by federal officials go to the U.S. Department of State.
U.S. Department of State: Request Authentication Services
Which state apostilles my birth certificate if I live in a different state now?

The state where the certificate was issued. Washington's Secretary of State, for example, says a birth certificate issued in another state must be apostilled in the state where the person was born. See the birth certificate guide.
Can my state apostille my FBI background check?

No. An FBI background check is a federal document, so the U.S. Department of State issues the apostille. Illinois, New York and Washington each say this on their official pages. See the FBI background check guide.
U.S. Department of State: Request Authentication Services
How long does a federal (FBI check) apostille take?

The U.S. Department of State says it processes mailed requests within 5 weeks of receipt, and walk-in drop-offs in Washington, DC within 7 business days. Mailing time is extra. Same-day service is only for a life-or-death emergency with travel within two weeks.
U.S. Department of State: Request Authentication Services
How much does an apostille cost?

Each office sets its own fee. Among the states this site covers so far, the official fee ranges from $2 per document (Illinois) to $25 per certificate (New Jersey); the U.S. Department of State charges $20 per document. Private services charge extra. Compare fees in the directory.
U.S. Department of State: Request Authentication Services
How long does a state apostille take?

It varies by state and season, and some offices don't publish a time at all. Published examples: Texas says up to two weeks by mail; Illinois 7 to 14 business days; Pennsylvania 5 to 7 business days after receipt. Each state page shows what the office itself publishes, and says so when it publishes nothing.
Texas SOS: Request a Universal Apostille
Do I need County Clerk certification before the state apostille?

In some states, yes. In New York, birth, death and marriage certificates issued by a local or county official, and all notarized documents, must be certified by the County Clerk first. Many other states don't have this step. Check your state's page.
Can I get an apostille on a photocopy?

Not on a plain photocopy. Offices apostille an original or a certified copy issued by the official record keeper. For documents like a passport, Washington says the copy must be notarized as a true copy by a notary.
How do I apostille a diploma or transcript?

The rules differ by state, so check the state where the school is located. Washington, for example, accepts official college transcripts signed by the registrar without notarization. North Carolina requires diplomas and transcripts to be notarized by a North Carolina notary, because a registrar's school seal alone is not accepted.
NC SOS: Process for Obtaining Authentication Certificates
What's the difference between an apostille and an authentication?

An apostille is used for countries that are party to the Hague Apostille Convention. For other countries, state offices generally issue a certificate of authentication instead. Depending on the country, it may also need further certification from the U.S. Department of State before the destination country's embassy or consulate legalizes it. See Hague countries.

The countries listed as contracting parties on the HCCH status table: 130 as of its June 30, 2026 update. Recent additions include China (in force November 7, 2023) and Canada (January 11, 2024). Check the table before you file, because the list changes.

No. The HCCH says a validly issued apostille has no expiry date and cannot be rejected only because of its age. The country receiving it may still require the underlying document (such as a background check or birth certificate) to be recently issued, so ask the receiving authority.
Do I need an apostille to use a document in another U.S. state?
No. Apostilles are for use abroad. Texas says it does not apostille documents for use within the United States, and Washington says its certificates are not valid for use within the U.S.
Texas SOS: Request a Universal Apostille
Should I translate before or after the apostille?

It depends on the receiving country, and no U.S. office sets one rule. The HCCH notes that a translator's notarized statement can itself be apostilled. Ask the authority that will receive your documents which order it wants before you pay for either.
Can a document notarized online (RON) be apostilled?

It depends on the state. Texas says online (RON) notarizations can be apostilled if they come with the notary's ledger details and a proper online-notarization certificate, and warns that some countries don't accept online-notarized documents. This site has not verified the rule for every state, so check with the state where the notary is commissioned and with the receiving authority.
